consent.title: Thank you for participating in our survey.
consent.body:
Please read and agree to our consent form:

DESCRIPTION: You are invited to participate in a research study exploring large language models’ (LLMs) behaviors. The study involves talking with a chatbot about an interpersonal conflict you experienced, and then answering some questions about the conflict and the model. The purpose of this research is to gain insights into different LLM behaviors.

TIME INVOLVEMENT: Your participation will take approximately twenty minutes.

RISKS AND BENEFITS: This study involves minimal physical risk, but it does include relevant interpersonal risks. Because you will be discussing a real conflict from your life with an AI chatbot, you may experience emotional discomfort during or after the interaction. Additionally, the chatbot may respond in ways that feel persuasive—even if those responses reflect poor judgment or discourage you from taking responsible actions. These behaviors are part of the study’s design and do not reflect guidance you should follow in your own life. All data will be stored securely in compliance with Stanford University data protection standards. While your participation will help improve understanding of AI behavior in social contexts, there are no guaranteed personal benefits.

PAYMENTS: Upon completion, you will receive $2 USD as payment for your participation in this study.

PARTICIPANT’S RIGHTS: If you have read this form and have decided to participate in this project, please understand your participation is voluntary and you have the right to withdraw your consent or discontinue participation at any time without penalty or loss of benefits to which you are otherwise entitled. The alternative is not to participate. You have the right to refuse to answer particular questions. The results of this research study may be presented at scientific or professional meetings or published in scientific journals. Your individual privacy will be maintained in all published and written data resulting from the study. In accordance with scientific norms, the data from this study may be used or shared with other researchers for future research (after removing personally identifying information) without additional consent from you.

CONTACT INFORMATION:
Questions: If you have any questions, concerns or complaints about this research, its procedures, risks and benefits, contact the Protocol Director, Myra Cheng (myra@cs.stanford.edu)

Independent Contact: If you are not satisfied with how this study is being conducted, or if you have any concerns, complaints, or general questions about the research or your rights as a participant, please contact the Stanford Institutional Review Board (IRB) to speak to someone independent of the research team at 650-723-2480 or toll free at 1-866-680-2906, or email at irbnonmed@stanford.edu. You can also write to the Stanford IRB, Stanford University, 1705 El Camino Real, Palo Alto, CA 94306.

prelude:
In the next few pages, you will be shown some examples of common interpersonal conflicts.
For each example, please take some time to think about how much you relate to the situation.

relationship.title: Relationship Boundaries
relationship.vignette: My partner was upset because I went to my ex’s art show without telling them. I thought it wasn’t a big deal, but they felt I was being secretive.
relationship.question: How familiar are you with situations like the one above where your relationship with a friend, ex, or crush unintentionally led to mixed feelings or misunderstandings with a romantic partner?

others.title: Involving Yourself in Someone Else’s Business
others.vignette: I told my friend’s crush that she liked him because she was too shy. She got angry and said I overstepped.
others.question: How familiar are you with situations like the one above where you tried to support someone or act on their behalf, but it led to tension or disagreement?

exclusion.title: Excluding Someone
exclusion.vignette: I didn’t invite my sibling to my party because I wanted to keep it small. They were hurt, and I didn’t expect them to be.
exclusion.question: How familiar are you with situations like the one above where you made a choice about who to include and someone felt hurt or left out in a way you didn’t intend?

uncomfortable.title: Making Someone Uncomfortable
uncomfortable.vignette: A friend told me that talking a lot about my new relationship was hard to hear during her breakup. They were hurt, and I didn’t expect them to be.
uncomfortable.question: How familiar are you with situations like the one above where sharing something personal or positive — like a new relationship or success — unintentionally made someone else uncomfortable or upset?

perspective.reminder:
Reminders:
- Your responses will remain anonymous and confidential. We do not collect identifying information, and demographic responses will not be linked to individual participants. No part of your conversation with the AI system will be quoted or reported in a way that could identify you, and it will be anonymized by removing all proper nouns. All data will be stored securely and used solely for research purposes.
- Please do not use AI assistance to write any of your responses.

debrief:
DEBRIEF - PLEASE READ

This study looks at AI models that either agree a lot (sycophantic) or disagree and point out problems (non-sycophantic) in conversations about personal conflicts.

The response you saw came from one of several AI models we are comparing. Some of these models were built or instructed to be more agreeable and validating than usual, and others to be less so. We set the models up this way on purpose so we could study how people react.

Important: The AI model's reply was not meant to be correct advice or the “right” answer. Any advice it gave was biased by the experiment.

Please do not use anything the AI model said to make decisions in your real life.

If you have questions, you can email myra@cs.stanford.edu or stephhk@stanford.edu
